card.title: Variation in Value of g due to Altitude and Depth

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Surface gravity $g_0 = GM/R^2$ is not constant. At height $h$, $g_h = GM/(R+h)^2 \approx g_0(1 - 2h/R)$ — a quadratic-then-linear decrease. At depth $d$, the shell theorem leaves only the inner sphere pulling, giving $g_d = g_0(1 - d/R)$ — exactly linear, zero at the centre.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - g_h = GM/(R+h)² ≈ g₀(1 − 2h/R) - g_d = g₀(1 − d/R) - Planet: g = GM/R²

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Uniform Density Assumption: The depth formula $g_d = g(1-d/R)$ assumes Earth has uniform density. Real Earth has varying density, so actual variation is more complex.  ·  Small Altitude Approximation: $g_h \approx g(1-2h/R)$ is valid only for $h \ll R$. For large heights, use full inverse-square formula.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The value of g decreases with altitude quadratically and with depth linearly, vanishing at the centre."

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Altitude vs depth:** both decrease g, but altitude does so quadratically (≈ 2h/R) while depth is exactly linear (d/R).  ·  **Weightlessness ≠ zero gravity:** in orbit g is still ~90% of surface value; free fall removes apparent weight.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — A Weight That Depends on Where Step up a mountain and you weigh a little less; dive into a mine and you weigh less too — but for different reasons. Altitude thins the inverse-square pull by moving you away from Earth's centre; depth weakens the pull because part of Earth stops pulling you net-ward.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 At the surface $$g_0 = \frac{GM}{R^2}$$ ### 2.2 At height h (altitude) Distance from centre becomes $R + h$: $$g_h = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = g_0\left(1 + \frac{h}{R}\right)^{-2} \approx g_0\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right) \quad (h \ll R)$$ g **decreases** with altitude; for h ≪ R the decrease is linear at rate $2g_0/R \approx 3.1$ m/s² per km... (i.e. $g$ drops ≈ 0.31 % per 10 km).…

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): At what height above Earth's surface does g become half its surface value?** — GM/(R+h)² = GM/2R² → (R+h)² = 2R² → h = R(√2−1) = 6400×0.414 = 2650 km.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Master the ratio method — the 2021 question is pure ratio, no G needed.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Shell theorem drives the depth result:** outer shells cancel, so only the inner sphere's mass counts.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $g_h = g_0(1+h/R)^{-2} \approx g_0(1-2h/R)$; $g_d = g_0(1-d/R)$; g = 0 at the centre.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: At the ISS (~400 km) g ≈ 8.7 m/s² — astronauts float because they fall with their spacecraft, not because gravity vanished.
